00001| //! Sentence scoping and command-policy classification for shell routing.
00002| //!
00003| //! A prompt that *mentions* a command is not a prompt that *asks for* one.
00004| //! Hive Mind wraps every Codex request in caller policy — *"When running sudo
00005| //! commands, run them in the background."* — and matching a run verb against a
00006| //! command token message-wide planned a bare `sudo` for every such run
00007| //! (issue #907). So routing reads one sentence at a time, and a sentence that
00008| //! only governs commands never licenses the token it names.
00009| //!
00010| //! This is the classification half of [`super::shell_command`]; the routing
00011| //! half calls [`sentence_spans`], [`states_a_command_policy`] and
00012| //! [`named_shell_command_in_sentence`].
00013| 
00014| use crate::seed::{self, TerminalCommandVocabulary};
00015| 
00016| /// One sentence of a prompt: its trimmed text, and the byte range it occupies.
00017| ///
00018| /// The ranges tile the prompt, so dropping a sentence and concatenating the rest
00019| /// reproduces the original wording verbatim — which is what a route needs when
00020| /// it consumes one clause of a request and hands the remainder on (issue #1066).
00021| pub(super) struct Sentence<'a> {
00022|     /// The sentence with its surrounding whitespace and terminator removed.
00023|     pub(super) text: &'a str,
00024|     /// Where the sentence sits in the prompt, terminator included.
00025|     pub(super) span: std::ops::Range<usize>,
00026| }
00027| /// The prompt split into sentences, with a semicolon ending one.
00028| ///
00029| /// Splitting keeps the original case and spacing, because a recovered command
00030| /// carries its arguments through verbatim — `run cat notes.txt` has to survive
00031| /// as one sentence, so a dot inside a token ends nothing, exactly as in
00032| /// [`sentences_with_mood`].
00033| ///
00034| /// A semicolon ends a sentence here because this is the scope shell routing
00035| /// reads at, and `build; deploy` names two commands to judge one at a time.
00036| /// Prose does not read it that way — see [`prose_sentences`].
00037| pub(super) fn sentences(prompt: &str) -> Vec<Sentence<'_>> {
00038|     split_sentences(prompt, |character| {
00039|         matches!(
00040|             character,
00041|             '.' | '!' | '?' | ';' | '\n' | '。' | '！' | '？' | '；' | '।'
00042|         )
00043|     })
00044| }
00045| /// The prompt split into sentences, with a semicolon joining rather than ending
00046| /// one.
00047| ///
00048| /// A semicolon separates two commands and joins two clauses, and which of those
00049| /// it does depends on who is reading. Bounding a literal write payload with the
00050| /// shell's reading truncated the payload at the first semicolon: issue #918's
00051| /// minimal-core invariant — *"… or a host surface; domain knowledge and policy
00052| /// belong in data."* — reached its file ending at *host surface;*, with the
00053| /// clause saying where domain knowledge goes dropped (issue #1066).
00054| ///
00055| /// Everything else about the split is the same, terminator handling included,
00056| /// because the two readings disagree about one character and nothing more.
00057| pub(super) fn prose_sentences(prompt: &str) -> Vec<Sentence<'_>> {
00058|     split_sentences(prompt, |character| {
00059|         matches!(character, '.' | '!' | '?' | '\n' | '。' | '！' | '？' | '।')
00060|     })
00061| }
00062| /// The prompt split wherever `ends_sentence` says a sentence ends.
00063| fn split_sentences(prompt: &str, ends_sentence: impl Fn(char) -> bool) -> Vec<Sentence<'_>> {
00064|     let mut sentences = Vec::new();
00065|     let mut span_start = 0;
00066|     let mut start = 0;
00067|     for (index, character) in prompt.char_indices() {
00068|         if !ends_sentence(character) {
00069|             continue;
00070|         }
00071|         if character == '.'
00072|             && prompt[index + character.len_utf8()..]
00073|                 .chars()
00074|                 .next()
00075|                 .is_some_and(char::is_alphanumeric)
00076|         {
00077|             continue;
00078|         }
00079|         let text = prompt[start..index].trim();
00080|         let end = index + character.len_utf8();
00081|         if !text.is_empty() {
00082|             sentences.push(Sentence {
00083|                 text,
00084|                 span: span_start..end,
00085|             });
00086|             span_start = end;
00087|         }
00088|         start = end;
00089|     }
00090|     let tail = prompt[start..].trim();
00091|     if !tail.is_empty() {
00092|         sentences.push(Sentence {
00093|             text: tail,
00094|             span: span_start..prompt.len(),
00095|         });
00096|     }
00097|     sentences
00098| }

00101|     sentences(prompt)
00102|         .into_iter()
00103|         .map(|sentence| sentence.text)
00104|         .collect()
00105| }
00106| /// Whether `sentence` states a *rule about* running commands rather than asking
00107| /// for one to run.

00110| /// *"When running sudo commands, run them in the background"* tells the agent how
00111| /// to treat a class of commands it may later choose to run. Nothing in it names a
00112| /// command to run now, so no token inside it may become one.
00113| pub(super) fn states_a_command_policy(sentence: &str) -> bool {
00114|     let lower = sentence.to_lowercase();
00115|     // A lead opens the rule, or qualifies it from the middle: *"Run commands
00116|     // with sudo only when necessary"* is as much a rule as *"When running sudo
00117|     // commands, …"*, and both name a class rather than an instance. The test
00118|     // itself lives on the vocabulary, because the same lead marks the same thing
00119|     // wherever it is read — web-search routing asks the same question of the
00120|     // topic a search marker introduces (issue #1066).
00121|     let carries_lead = seed::caller_context_vocabulary().carries_policy_lead(&lower);

00123|     // real requests carry one, and treating them as policy answers nothing at
00124|     // all, which is strictly worse than answering imperfectly.
00125|     //
00126|     // The separator is *where* a command is named. A conditional clause runs to
00127|     // its comma; whatever follows is the order the condition qualifies. So
00128|     // *"If the build fails, run cargo test."* orders `cargo test` after the
00129|     // condition and routes, while *"When running sudo commands, run them in the
00130|     // background."* names only a pronoun there — it is telling the agent how to
00131|     // treat a class of commands, not asking for one. A rule with no comma at all
00132|     // (*"Never run rm outside the workspace."*) governs throughout and orders
00133|     // nothing.
00134|     carries_lead
00135|         && lower
00136|             .split_once(',')

00138| }
00139| 
00140| /// Whether `clause` orders a concrete command: a run verb immediately followed
00141| /// by a known shell token. This is the difference between asking for a command
00142| /// and talking about commands.
00143| fn orders_a_named_command(clause: &str) -> bool {
00144|     let vocab = seed::terminal_command_vocabulary();
00145|     let words: Vec<&str> = clause.split_whitespace().collect();
00146|     words.iter().enumerate().any(|(index, word)| {
00147|         let is_verb = vocab
00148|             .run_verbs
00149|             .iter()
00150|             .any(|verb| verb == &normalize_command_word(word));

00152|             && words.get(index + 1).is_some_and(|next| {
00153|                 let token = normalize_command_word(next);
00154|                 vocab.shell_tokens.iter().any(|known| known == &token)
00155|             })
00156|     })
00157| }
00158| 
00159| /// Whether every sentence of `prompt` is caller policy, so nothing in it asks
00160| /// for a command to run now.
00161| ///
00162| /// The check is whole-prompt because `prefixed_shell_command` claims a message
00163| /// that merely *starts* with `run`/`execute` before any sentence-level rule is
00164| /// consulted; a policy filter applied only to `named_shell_command` would leave
00165| /// that branch open. Requiring *every* sentence to be policy keeps a genuine
00166| /// request that arrives alongside one — *"Never run rm outside the workspace.
00167| /// Now run git status."* — reaching the router through its second sentence.

00169| /// A conditional request keeps working, because [`states_a_command_policy`]
00170| /// asks whether the sentence names a command rather than only how it opens:
00171| /// *"If the build fails, run cargo test."* names `cargo` and routes, while the
00172| /// reported *"When running sudo commands, run them in the background."* names
00173| /// only a pronoun and does not.
00174| pub(super) fn governs_commands_rather_than_requesting_one(prompt: &str) -> bool {
00175|     let sentences = sentence_spans(prompt);
00176|     !sentences.is_empty() && sentences.iter().all(|sentence| states_a_command_policy(sentence))

00178| 
00179| /// The command text after a passthrough prefix, past an optional colon.
00180| ///
00181| /// A leading code span is the command and the words after it are prose
00182| /// (``Run `node --test x.test.js` and tell me …``, PR #1188 G76); with no
00183| /// leading span, a remainder whose backticks do not pair is no command (the
00184| /// shell would read a command substitution), so `None` (mirrors
00185| /// `commandSpan`).
00186| pub(super) fn command_span(remainder: &str) -> Option<&str> {
00187|     let text = remainder
00188|         .strip_prefix(':')
00189|         .unwrap_or(remainder)
00190|         .trim_start();
00191|     let fence = &text[..text.len() - text.trim_start_matches('`').len()];

00193|         && let Some(close) = text[fence.len()..].find(fence)
00194|     {
00195|         let inner = text[fence.len()..fence.len() + close].trim();
00196|         if !inner.is_empty() && !inner.contains('`') {
00197|             return Some(inner);
00198|         }
00199|     }
00200|     text.matches('`').count().is_multiple_of(2).then_some(text)
00201| }

00206| ) -> Option<String> {
00207|     let lower = prompt.to_ascii_lowercase();

00209|     let has_cjk_verb = vocab.cjk_run_verbs.iter().any(|v| lower.contains(v));

00212|     // (paths, flags, filenames) survive intact.
00213|     let words: Vec<&str> = prompt
00214|         .split(|c: char| c.is_whitespace())
00215|         .filter(|w| !w.is_empty())
00216|         .collect();
00217| 
00218|     let is_run_verb = |word: &str| {
00219|         let normalized = normalize_command_word(word);
00220|         vocab.run_verbs.iter().any(|v| v == &normalized)
00221|     };

00223|         let normalized = normalize_command_word(word);
00224|         !normalized.is_empty() && vocab.shell_tokens.iter().any(|t| t == &normalized)
00225|     };
00226|     let has_verb = words.iter().any(|w| is_run_verb(w)) || has_cjk_verb;
00227| 
00228|     // Shape 1: a shell token directly after a run verb — the command plus its arguments.
00229|     for (index, word) in words.iter().enumerate() {
00230|         if index == 0 || !is_shell_token(word) {
00231|             continue;
00232|         }
00233|         if is_run_verb(words[index - 1]) {
00234|             return Some(collect_command(&words[index..]));
00235|         }
00236|     }

00238|     // Shape 2: a shell token named as a command -- written as code, or right
00239|     // after a seeded command noun (`run the command ls`) -- given run context,
00240|     // the token alone. A shell word elsewhere in the sentence is prose: `Create
00241|     // a Python test … and run it` names no `python` command (PR #1188 G25).
00242|     let named_as_command = |index: usize, word: &str| {
00243|         is_shell_token(word)

00246|                     vocab
00247|                         .command_nouns
00248|                         .contains(&words[previous].to_ascii_lowercase())
00249|                 }))
00250|     };

00253|             .iter()
00254|             .enumerate()
00255|             .find(|(index, word)| named_as_command(*index, word))
